meta.blurb: In the glittering, rule-bound New York of the 1870s, a young lawyer is about to marry the perfect bride when her mysterious cousin walks into the opera. Newland Archer must choose between duty and desire, and between two women who see him very differently.
meta.bible: Newland Archer: a young New York lawyer, from an old family, thoughtful, restless and well-mannered. May Welland: his fiancée and later his wife, pretty, kind, loyal, apparently innocent but wiser than she seems. Ellen Olenska: May's cousin, the Countess Olenska, who has left her husband and returned from Europe; honest, charming and unconventional. Count Olenski: Ellen's Polish husband, who never appears. Mrs Welland: May's mother. Mr Welland: May's father. Mrs Manson Mingott: the huge, fearless grandmother of May and Ellen. Mrs Archer: Newland's mother. Janey: Newland's sister. Julius Beaufort: a rich, charming banker whose bank fails. Regina Beaufort: his wife. Sillerton Jackson: an old man who knows all the gossip. Lawrence Lefferts: a fashionable society man. Mr Letterblair: the old family lawyer who employs Archer. Henry van der Luyden and Louisa van der Luyden: the most respected couple in New York society. Monsieur Rivière: a Frenchman, the Count's secretary, who helped Ellen to escape. Dallas: Archer's eldest son. Fanny Beaufort: Julius Beaufort's daughter, who marries Dallas. Academy of Music: the New York opera house. Faust: the opera. Grace Church: where May and Archer marry. St Augustine: the town in Florida where May spends the winter. Newport: the seaside resort. Boston, Paris, Europe, Florida, New York, Washington. Metropolitan Museum. Invalides: the golden dome in Paris near Ellen's home. Voice and tone: elegant, gently ironic and sad; the rules of society are never spoken aloud; the love between Archer and Ellen is never consummated, and there is no violence; the ending is quiet and bitter-sweet.

B1B2: In New York in the 1870s, young Newland Archer arrives late at the opera, as fashion requires. In one of the boxes he sees May Welland, the young woman he is going to marry, dressed all in white.
Next to May sits a dark-haired woman in a plain dark gown. She is May's cousin, Ellen, Countess Olenska, who has just come back from Europe, and the whole theatre is whispering about her.
Everyone knows that Ellen left her husband, a rich Polish count, and that the marriage ended badly. Old New York families dislike scandal, so they fear that she will bring trouble to them all.
Archer goes into the box, greets May's family and shakes hands with Ellen. He decides to ask May to announce their engagement that very night, to show that the family is united.
At the Beauforts' ball that night, May tells her friends that they are engaged. Everyone is delighted, and Archer feels proud and pleased with himself.
Ellen arrives late at the ball, and several guests give her cold looks. Archer goes to her at once, and he welcomes her warmly, as one of his own family.
Newland lives with his mother and his sister Janey in a quiet, tidy house. In their world everyone is polite, and nobody says aloud anything that might cause a scandal.
May's grandmother, old Mrs Mingott, is very large and very bold, and she does not care what society says. She laughs at the gossip, and she welcomes Ellen into her house.
The van der Luydens are the most respected people in New York society. Archer asks them to help Ellen, and they agree to invite her to dinner.
At the dinner, the guests are polite to Ellen, and her place in society is saved. Archer is glad, but he is surprised by how much he cares about her.
Ellen lives in a small house in an unfashionable street, and Archer calls on her there. The rooms are full of foreign treasures, and nothing in them looks like the houses of his friends.
Ellen tells Archer, with a smile, that New York hides the truth behind good manners. Her honest words make him look at his own comfortable world in a new way.
Mr Letterblair, the family lawyer, shows Archer some letters about Ellen's husband. The family fears the scandal of a divorce, so he asks the young man to change her mind.
Archer visits Ellen and urges her to give up the idea of a divorce for the sake of her family. She sadly agrees, and he feels ashamed of how easily he has won.
Archer thinks of Ellen more and more, and he cannot stop. He knows that it is wrong, because he has promised to marry May, who is good and loves him.
Archer travels south to St Augustine in Florida, where May is spending the winter. He begs her to marry him sooner, but she says that a proper engagement must last longer.
May looks at him carefully and says that if he loves another woman, he is free to say so. He answers that there is no one, and she smiles, although she does not seem fully sure.
A Frenchman named Monsieur Rivière arrives with a message from Ellen's husband, who wants her back. Ellen refuses, and Rivière tells Archer privately that he himself helped her to escape.
When Ellen leaves for Boston, Archer follows her and finds her in a public garden. They speak honestly of their feelings, but Ellen says that they must never hurt May.
Archer hopes that marriage will end his doubts, so he asks May's parents to choose an early date. They agree after a little complaining, and May is delighted by the news.
Archer and May are married in a grand church wedding, and all of New York society comes to watch. Afterwards the young couple sail for Europe, where they will spend their honeymoon.
On their honeymoon in Europe, May is cheerful and kind and enjoys every sight. She never asks a difficult question, and Archer finds that he has little to say to her.
Back in New York, Archer returns to his law work and to the dinners and calls of society. May is a perfect wife, and their days follow a quiet, regular pattern.
At Newport, May wins the archery prize in a white dress, and everyone claps for her. Then Archer sees Ellen arriving late across the lawn, and his heart jumps.
At Newport, Archer finds Ellen sitting alone and looking at the sea. He tells himself that he will go to her if she turns before a boat passes the lighthouse, but she never turns.
When winter comes, Archer sees Ellen often in the company of the rich banker Julius Beaufort. People are talking, and Archer is surprised by how jealous he feels.
Julius Beaufort's bank suddenly fails, and he is ruined. The same people who once went to his parties now turn their backs on him and his wife.
Old Mrs Mingott has a stroke, and the whole family hurries to her bedside. Ellen comes to look after her grandmother, and Archer sees her there once more.
Archer and Ellen meet in an almost empty museum and speak of love at last. He asks her to run away with him, but she says it would hurt too many people.
In a closed carriage Ellen tells Archer that she will not be his secret love. She says that she can only go on loving him if she gives him up.
Archer goes home to May, who is gentle and trusting and knows nothing of his secret. He feels trapped between his duty to her and his love for Ellen.
Ellen tells Archer that she has decided to go back to Europe, far from them all. He says that he will find a way to follow her.
Before Archer can speak of leaving, May tells him she is going to have a baby. She adds quietly that she told Ellen two weeks ago, and he understands why Ellen has decided to go.
May arranges a big farewell dinner for Ellen, and all the great families of New York come. Everyone is kind and smiling, and Archer sits at the table feeling more and more strange.
At the dinner Archer suddenly understands that everyone has known about his love for Ellen. The families have quietly joined together to keep him with May, and he is their prisoner.
Not long after the dinner, Ellen sails back to Europe, and the ship soon leaves the harbour. Archer lets her go, knowing that he has lost the only woman he has ever truly loved.
Soon May's baby is born, a boy called Dallas. Archer finds that being a father fills the emptiness in his life, at least a little.
The years go by, and Archer becomes a respected citizen who works for good causes. Meanwhile New York changes, and many of the old rules are quietly forgotten.
May becomes seriously ill after caring for one of their sick children, and she dies. Archer mourns her sincerely, for she was a good wife and a good mother.
Dallas is going to marry Fanny Beaufort, the daughter of the ruined banker. Years ago this would have shocked society, but now nobody seems to mind.
Before the wedding, Archer and his son visit Paris. Dallas says that he has arranged for them to visit the Countess Olenska, and Archer is amazed.
Dallas tells his father quietly that his mother once spoke to him about the past. She said that Archer had given up the thing he most wanted, when she asked him to, and that she trusted him.
Archer stops in the middle of the street, so surprised and moved that he cannot speak. All those years May knew about his secret love, and she never said one word.
Archer and Dallas walk through the afternoon sunshine toward the Countess's home. The gold dome of the Invalides shines over the roofs, and Archer's steps become slower.
Dallas points up at a high balcony and says that the Countess lives there. Archer stops in the square, unable to take another step.
Archer sits down on a bench and tells Dallas to go up without him. Dallas is surprised, but he sees his father's face and does not argue.
Dallas goes into the building, and Archer stays on the bench looking up at the balcony. He imagines Ellen there, pouring tea for his son, and he is silent.

Archer sits very still on the bench and thinks about everything that has happened in his life. He feels that Ellen is more real to him in his memory, here on the bench, than she would be if he went upstairs.
After a while a servant steps onto the balcony and closes the shutters. Archer watches the last light leave the window, and he knows that the visit has ended.
Archer gets up from the bench and walks back to his hotel alone. The evening lamps of Paris are coming on, and he feels strangely at peace.
C1C2: On a winter evening in the New York of the 1870s, young Newland Archer strolled into the opera house late, as every gentleman of fashion was expected to do. From the back of the club box he looked across the glittering horseshoe of the theatre and saw May Welland, the girl he was soon to marry, seated in her family's box in a gown of spotless white. She seemed to him the very picture of purity, and he felt a quiet, proprietary pleasure at the thought that she would soon be his wife.

Beside May, half hidden by the shadow of the curtain, sat a slender, dark-haired woman in a gown far plainer than fashion allowed. She was Ellen Olenska, May's cousin, who had lately returned to New York after many years in Europe, and Archer felt the eyes of the whole house turn upon her. He understood at once that her arrival, in the family's own box, on such a night, was a kind of challenge.

Round the club box, old Sillerton Jackson and the other men who knew everything about everyone murmured that Ellen had left her husband, a rich Polish count, and run away from his house in Europe. In the New York of those days a woman who left her husband was a danger to every family she touched, however cruel he might have been. The old families preferred silence and appearances to the truth, and they were already wondering how the whole affair might be hushed.

Archer crossed the house to the Mingott box, where May greeted him with a shy, happy smile and Ellen gave him a frank and friendly hand. It struck him suddenly that the best way to protect May's cousin from gossip was to make the engagement public at once, and so tie the whole family together in the eyes of the world. He told May of his plan, and she answered with the quick, generous understanding that he loved in her.

At the Beauforts' ball later that evening, the engagement was made known, and congratulations rained upon the young couple from every side. Mrs Welland pretended to be annoyed at the haste, though in her heart she was delighted, and May blushed and smiled with perfect grace. Archer, standing in the glittering ballroom, felt that his life had been settled most agreeably, and he did not guess how soon that feeling would change.

Ellen arrived late, in a dark gown, and a ripple of disapproval passed through the ballroom as the ladies noted her presence and looked away. Archer, mindful of the family he was about to join, went to her at once and greeted her with a warmth that a cousin-to-be could not be accused of overdoing. She thanked him with her eyes, and he felt the pleasure of a man who has done a generous deed and been rewarded with more than he deserved.

At home, Newland lived with his mother and his sister Janey, two gentle women who knew every rule of old New York and obeyed it without complaint. Their world was polite, comfortable and orderly, and what mattered most in it was that certain things should never be said, because to speak of them would make them real. Newland loved his family and respected its customs, yet he sometimes wondered whether anyone had ever stepped outside the pattern to see what lay beyond.

May's grandmother, old Mrs Mingott, was an enormous, fearless old woman who had outlived her husband and most of her fears, and she ruled her family from a great armchair. She laughed at the gossip, praised the engagement, and made it plain that she meant to keep her granddaughter Ellen near her, in spite of what the neighbours thought. Her shrewd eyes seemed to see through Archer's good manners, and he left the house feeling that she knew more about his heart than he did.

The van der Luydens, cousins of the Archers, were the most dignified and respected family in New York, and their approval could make or unmake any reputation. Archer's family persuaded them that Ellen deserved their protection, and, with grave and solemn kindness, they agreed to invite her to a dinner. It was a small favour, but in that world a dinner invitation from such a house was as decisive as the verdict of a court.

At the van der Luydens' table, Ellen sat serenely among the stiff old guests, and her calm grace did more for her reputation than any argument could have done. The doors of New York, which had threatened to close against her, now stood politely open, and Archer was relieved that his plan had worked. Yet he noticed, with a vague alarm, that his relief was warmer than a friend's care for his future wife's cousin ought to be.

Ellen had taken a small house in an unfashionable street, among dressmakers and artists whom the best families did not visit. Archer, who called on her there one afternoon, found rooms full of dim lamps, Eastern rugs and strange flowers, and a charm that nothing in his orderly world resembled. She spoke of Europe lightly and of New York with a frank curiosity that made him feel, for the first time, how small the horizon of his own life was.

Ellen told him, with a smile that held more pain than amusement, that she had found New York kind but that its kindness was a way of hiding everything it did not wish to see. Her honest words fell on Archer like a draught of cold air in a stuffy room, and he began to look at his own comfortable world through her curious, foreign eyes. He found that May's cheerful certainty, which he had always admired, seemed suddenly a little narrow.

In the dusty law office where Archer worked, old Mr Letterblair laid before him a packet of papers from Count Olenski's lawyers, with an air of serious regret. Ellen wished to divorce her husband, he explained, and the family feared that the scandal would damage them all, and so he begged that Archer, as a future relation, would reason with her. Archer accepted the task confidently, believing that it was simply his duty to help the people he was about to join.

Archer called on Ellen and urged her, in the name of the family and of old New York, to abandon her wish for a divorce. She listened with her eyes lowered, and then, sadly and without anger, said that if that was what her friends thought best, she would yield. He went away feeling that he had done something small and unworthy, and that she had been wiser than he.

Through the weeks that followed, Archer found that his thoughts turned to Ellen at every idle moment, and he could not drive her image from his mind however firmly he tried. He reminded himself that May was good, loving and utterly trustworthy, and that he had given her his word. Yet the more he praised May's innocence to himself, the more it seemed like a wall, and the more he longed to climb over it.

Hoping to escape his own confusion, Archer travelled south to St Augustine, where May was spending the winter with her parents in the sunshine of Florida. He begged her to bring the wedding forward, but she answered, with gentle firmness, that her family expected a proper engagement and that she could not hurry them. He was moved by her sweetness and exasperated by her obedience, and he could not tell which feeling was the stronger.

With a sudden directness that surprised him, May said that if he had ever come to love another woman, he must tell her, and she would not stand in his way. Archer, startled, answered that there was no one, and she accepted his word with a smile that was brave and perhaps not wholly convinced. In that moment he saw that her innocence concealed a depth of generosity that he had never suspected, and he felt ashamed.

A Frenchman, Monsieur Rivière, arrived from Europe with an offer from Ellen's husband, who wished to have his wife returned to him. Ellen refused to go, and Rivière confided to Archer, with tears in his eyes, that it was he who had helped her escape and that she should never go back. Archer listened with a strange mixture of sympathy and joy, for it meant that she was free to remain, and near him.

When Ellen slipped away to Boston, Archer followed her on the next train, and found her sitting alone in the Public Garden beside the still water. For the first time they spoke openly of what lay between them, and each saw the same longing in the other's eyes. Yet Ellen would not allow him to break his promise to May, and the two parted with their hearts full and their lips sealed.

Believing that marriage would cure his restlessness, as a strong wall holds back a flood, Archer pressed the Wellands to name an early date. After the usual protests about dresses and tradition, they gave way, and May received the news with a radiance that made him feel both guilty and relieved. The wedding was fixed for the spring, and Archer told himself that his duty and his happiness were now one and the same.

The wedding was everything that New York could wish, with the whole of society gathered in Grace Church to watch May walk up the aisle on her father's arm. Archer stood at the altar with a smile that he hoped looked as happy as it was meant to, while some part of him quietly wondered how the day had come so fast. That evening the young couple left for a long honeymoon in Europe, and the great chapter of his life that he had so often imagined at last began.

On the long honeymoon through Europe, May was cheerful, sweet-tempered and tireless in her enjoyment of every sight and every shop. She never asked a difficult question or doubted an opinion, and Archer, who had imagined opening for her the doors of a larger world, discovered that she had no wish to go through them. He began to feel, with a sinking heart, that he had married a charming stranger who would never become anything else.

Home in New York once more, the Archers fell into the smooth routine of dinners, calls and Sunday visits that their families expected of them. May managed their house with perfect taste, and Archer went to his office each morning, loyal in conduct, though not in thought. The days passed pleasantly, and yet he felt, now and then, as though he were walking round and round the inside of a very pretty cage.

At a summer party at Newport, May drew her bow with calm skill and won the prize, looking as fresh and fair as a goddess in her white dress. The guests applauded, and Archer was proud of her, until his eye caught a figure crossing the lawn late and alone, in a grey gown, with the sea light behind her. In an instant the applause seemed to come from far away, and he knew that nothing in his heart had changed.

One summer afternoon at Newport, Archer came upon Ellen sitting on a veranda with her back to him, gazing at the sea. He resolved that if she turned her head before a distant sailing boat passed the lighthouse, he would go to her, and he waited, motionless and tense, while the boat slid slowly by. She did not turn, and he went away, half relieved and half desolate, with the impression that fate had decided the matter for him.

When winter came, Archer saw that Ellen was often to be found in the company of Julius Beaufort, the wealthy banker whose charm and loose morals were known to everyone. The whispers of society began to follow her once more, and Archer, though he said nothing, burned with a jealousy that astonished him. It was bitter to realise that a married man had no right to such a feeling, and that his wife's cousin owed him nothing.

Without warning, Julius Beaufort's bank failed, and with it went his fortune, his credit and every claim he had on the respect of old New York. The same people who had danced in his ballrooms now turned their backs, and his wife Regina sought help from her relatives and found few friends willing to stand beside her. The society that had flattered her husband in his prosperity showed no mercy in his fall.

Not long afterwards old Mrs Mingott suffered a stroke, and the family hurried to her bedside as though afraid that a pillar of the house had fallen. Ellen came to nurse her grandmother day and night, and her devotion softened even the sternest critics. Archer, meeting her again in that quiet sickroom, felt that all the months of careful distance fell away like a thin coat of ice.

In the great, nearly empty halls of the Metropolitan Museum, Archer and Ellen met by arrangement and spoke at last of what both had long felt. He begged her to go away with him and begin a life of their own, but she answered that such happiness would be built on the suffering of others. Her eyes were full of tears, and yet her voice never wavered, and he understood that her mind was made up.

Alone together in a closed carriage, Archer asked her to be his, and Ellen answered that she would not live in secret and deceit, for she had seen too much of such lives in Europe. She told him that she could go on loving him only so long as she gave him up, because to take what he offered would spoil the very thing that made it precious. He sat silent in the dark, and both of them knew that every word she said was true.

That evening Archer returned to May, who greeted him with the same tender trust she had always shown and asked no questions at all. He sat beside her in the lamplight and felt himself divided into two men, one who obeyed every duty of a husband and another who longed with all his soul for Ellen. The house around him, with its fine furniture and soft carpets, seemed suddenly very quiet.

At last Ellen told him that she had decided to return to Europe, where she could live free of the gossip and the sorrow that clung to her in New York. Archer, desperate not to lose her, answered that he would follow, whatever the world might say and whatever he might leave behind. She did not argue, but she looked at him with an expression of tender doubt, as though she knew that the future would be shaped by forces larger than their wishes.

Just as Archer gathered his courage to speak of leaving, May looked up from her chair and told him, with shy happiness, that she was going to have a child. She had not been certain two weeks earlier, she said, when she had told Ellen so, but now she was sure. Archer understood in a moment that this was why Ellen had decided to go, and that his own plan had ended before he could even speak of it.

May gave a farewell dinner for Ellen, and all the great families of New York came to say goodbye, with a kindness that seemed warm and a politeness that seemed wholly sincere. Candles glittered on silver and flowers, the guests spoke of travel and weather, and Ellen sat at the centre of it with the composed, brilliant smile of a woman who had learned never to show her pain. Archer, at the end of the table, watched the scene as though he were observing it from behind thick glass.

As the dinner went on, Archer realised with a strange chill that the entire company knew of his love for Ellen, and that they had been acting together for weeks to keep him where he belonged. Every gentle smile and every careful remark had been part of the same quiet plan, and May herself, with her calm eyes, was at its centre. He felt like a man encircled by a ring of silent, friendly, immovable walls, and he understood that there was no way out.

Soon afterwards Ellen sailed for Europe, and Archer, who had once vowed to follow her anywhere, let her go without a word. He stood at the window of his house and watched the world continue in its ordinary way, as though nothing at all had been taken from him. It was the end of the only passion of his life, and it had ended not in drama but in silence.

Soon afterwards May gave birth to a son, whom they named Dallas, and Archer found in the child's small hands a comfort he had not expected to find. Two more children followed, and the house filled with the noise and bustle of family life that he had always been told was the true purpose of a man's existence. He did his duty with warmth and honesty, and if there was a corner of his heart that he kept closed, no one but himself ever knew.

The years passed, and Archer became a useful and respected citizen, serving on committees and supporting reforms that were good rather than brilliant. Around him, New York was changing beyond recognition, as tall buildings rose and new fortunes arrived and the old rules that had governed his youth gradually loosened their hold. He sometimes thought that he had lived in the last age of a world that no longer existed, and he was surprised to find that he did not mind.

May died suddenly of a fever she had caught while nursing one of their children, and her death left Archer a widower. He mourned her sincerely, for in all the years of their marriage she had never failed in kindness, duty or loyalty, and he had come to respect her more than he had once thought possible. At her grave he felt the sorrow of a man who has lost a good companion, though not the one he had once dreamed of.

Archer's eldest son Dallas announced that he was to marry Fanny Beaufort, the daughter of the very banker whose fall had once scandalised the whole city. In Archer's youth the match would have been unthinkable, and the families would have whispered for months, yet now no one seemed to care about old disgraces. He watched his son's happy face and realised how much freer the young were than his own generation had ever been.

Before the wedding, Archer and Dallas travelled together to Paris, a city Archer had not seen for many years. On the second day Dallas announced, with a light-hearted air, that he had arranged for them to call on the Countess Olenska that very afternoon. Archer felt his heart give a great, unsteady jump, as though a door long closed had opened without warning.

As they walked, Dallas told his father in a gentle voice that his mother had spoken to him, shortly before her death, about the past. She had said that Archer had once given up the thing he most wanted, because she had asked him, and that she had always trusted him for it. The young man spoke without embarrassment, in the easy, honest manner of a generation that had never been taught to hide its feelings.

Archer stopped in the street, struck dumb by what he had heard, for in all their years of marriage May had never given him the least hint of her knowledge. She had known everything and had borne it in silence, and she had trusted him to behave as honour required, as he had done. He felt a late and painful admiration for her quiet strength, and a sorrow that it had been spent on a love that was never wholly hers.

They crossed the great city in the warm afternoon sunshine, past fountains and bookstalls and the golden dome of the Invalides shining above the rooftops. Archer walked more and more slowly, as though each step carried him not toward a house but backward through three decades of time. He thought of the young man who had once stood at the back of an opera box, so certain of his future, and he almost laughed at his own innocence.

At last Dallas stopped in the square and pointed to a balcony high on one of the tall buildings, saying that the Countess lived up there. Archer looked at the sun-blinds and the shuttered windows and felt that he could not move, as though the pavement under his feet had turned into the whole of his past. He said, with a faint smile, that he would sit for a while on a bench, and that Dallas should go up alone.

Archer lowered himself onto a bench in the square and told Dallas, in the lightest tone he could manage, that he was too old-fashioned for such a visit and that his son should go up in his place. Dallas stared at him with surprise and some tenderness, then glanced at his father's face and understood that no argument would be of any use. The young man shrugged, smiled and crossed the square, and Archer was left alone with the afternoon.

Dallas disappeared through the doorway, and Archer sat looking up at the balcony, picturing the room beyond it, the lamps, the books, the woman who had been so many years in his thoughts. He imagined her welcoming his son with the frank, kind smile that he remembered so well, and wondering what had been said of her. A great quiet settled over him, and the ordinary noises of the square seemed to come from a long way off.

He sat motionless and understood that the love of his life had never been something to possess but something to remember, and that he had kept it alive precisely by never letting it be spoiled by the world. Ellen, in his mind, was young, dark-eyed and brave as she had been in the opera box, and she was more real to him there than any older woman could be. He had lived all his years without her, yet he had never been entirely without her, and that was enough.

After a while a servant stepped onto the balcony and began to close the shutters, one by one, against the lengthening sunlight. Archer watched the wooden leaves swing shut, and it seemed to him that a long and unspoken chapter of his life was closing with them. He sat a moment longer in the cooling air, and then he rose slowly, a little stiff, like a man who has finished a journey.

Archer turned and walked slowly back toward his hotel through the soft Paris dusk, past lighted cafes and the long avenues where the first lamps were beginning to glow. He did not look back at the balcony, for he had no need to, since everything that had mattered to him lay behind him already in the ordered silence of his memory. Dallas would give his account that evening, and Archer would listen gravely, and the age of innocence would remain, as it always had, a thing that could not be returned to.
